newsitem.title: JORDAN: King Hussein says army should have shot soldier.
newsitem.headline: King Hussein says army should have shot soldier.

text.p: King Hussein has told his army that a Jordanian soldier who gunned down seven Israeli schoolgirls last week should have been shot dead on the spot.

In a message sent to the armed forces before his departure for the United States on Friday, the king also rebuked the soldier's superior officers for not preventing his rampage at Baqoura on the Jordanian-Israeli border.
"The atrocious incident at Baqoura is one of the ugliest that we have lived (through)," the king said in a letter released on Thursday.
"It is a mark of shame on all who were directly responsible for the perpetrator, and all who saw him in his act and did not kill him immediately," he said.

"If there is any good to be derived from his survival, then it may come from the inquiry that will uncover the causes that pushed him to render this distinguished service to all the enemies of the Jordanian armed forces," the king added.
King Hussein's letter was the latest expression of shame for last Thursday's shooting, but his remorse has not been shared by all Jordanians.

Riot police had to set up a roadblock on Monday to prevent dozens of sympathisers of the soldier, Ahmed Mousa al-Daqamsa, from converging on his village in northern Jordan to pay respects to his family.
They said Daqamsa had been spurred on by a "burning rage" with Israel and said they were campaigning for a fair trial. Villagers told reporters Daqamsa had become a local hero.

Many Jordanians are disillusioned that a treaty with Israel signed in 1994 has failed to bring a promised "peace dividend" in terms of economic benefits. Israeli plans to build Jewish homes in Arab East Jerusalem and a limited West Bank withdrawal have increased hostility.
King Hussein warned the army to be vigilant to prevent "any treacherous or hateful agent from infiltrating our ranks to strike with our arms".
"We do not betray people with whom we have made peace," said the king, who last week visited Jerusalem to offer condolences to the families of the seven victims.

Jordanian television showed pictures of the king kneeling beside the relatives, next to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, just one week after he had harshly criticised Netanyahu for pushing the Middle East "towards an abyss of bloodshed."
Some Israeli ministers had suggested that Daqamsa was encouraged to act by the king's dark warning.
